title: Immigration and asylum: protection, returns and safe routes
label: 11 November 2026 · Immigration and asylum
summary: The committee examined the Government’s immigration and asylum proposals with representatives of UNHCR, the UN Refugee Agency, and the International Organization for Migration. The witnesses supported faster, fairer asylum decisions, returns for people who don’t need protection, and more safe routes, but questioned whether several measures would deter dangerous journeys. They warned that long waits for settlement, repayment of support and changes to modern-slavery protections could harm refugees and trafficking victims, and urged practical improvements and fair oversight instead.

chapters.title: The overall policy package
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses backed a well-run asylum system but questioned whether tougher rules would deter arrivals, and warned they could weaken refugee protection.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What do you think of the Government’s package as a whole? It aims to deter arrivals and speed up removals of people who have no right to stay.

turns.speaker: Vicky Tennant
turns.text: UNHCR, the UN Refugee Agency, supports the Government’s concern about dangerous journeys and the need to maintain public confidence in asylum. We welcome efforts to reduce the backlog, improve decisions, return people found not to need protection, and reopen resettlement and sponsorship routes.

turns.speaker: Vicky Tennant
turns.text: But there’s limited evidence that some of the proposed restrictions will change people’s decisions to travel. We’re more concerned that they could reduce the protection refugees receive, make it harder to settle and reunite families, and work against the Government’s aims of integration and independence.

turns.speaker: Vicky Tennant
turns.text: Safe routes need to grow, and family reunion should be restored. The UK should also work with other countries to address why people are moving. Access to asylum must remain available to people who arrive and ask for protection.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Does the International Organization for Migration broadly agree?

turns.speaker: Christa Rottensteiner
turns.text: Yes. A well-managed system matters. IOM has recorded 29 deaths this year among people travelling from mainland Europe to the UK. Safe routes are important, but they need to be part of a wider response to dangerous journeys.

turns.speaker: Christa Rottensteiner
turns.text: Our main concerns are the Bill’s modern-slavery rules. They could make it harder to identify and support victims, including UK nationals, who are the largest group recorded in the referral system. We also question whether the changes are needed, since many issues are already covered by existing law.

chapters.title: Temporary status and long waits
chapters.takeaway: UNHCR said some refugees could wait up to 30 years for permanent status, far longer than comparable routes in Denmark, with risks to their ability to build a life.

turns.speaker: Baroness Hamwee
turns.text: Under the proposed earned-settlement rules, some refugees could wait 30 years before applying for permanent status. How does that compare with other countries, and is it fair to refugees?

turns.speaker: Vicky Tennant
turns.text: Some refugees may move quickly into work or study routes. But people who can’t do that could face a wait of up to 30 years, making the UK an outlier. In Denmark, the usual route is eight years, or four for people who meet employment, income and language requirements.

turns.speaker: Vicky Tennant
turns.text: Denmark also reviews refugees’ status regularly. Those reviews rarely lead to people losing protection, because it’s unusual for conditions in their home country to change enough for a safe return. The reviews take time and resources, while uncertainty can make it harder for refugees to study, work and put down roots.

turns.speaker: Vicky Tennant
turns.text: Australia moved away from temporary protection towards permanent-residency routes, in part because of the human impact and the cost of repeatedly reviewing people’s cases. Protection should be temporary only in the sense that it leads to a lasting solution.

turns.speaker: Vicky Tennant
turns.text: The refugee convention says countries should make every effort to help refugees become citizens. A very long wait, combined with rules that could prevent people who arrived irregularly from becoming citizens, raises concerns about whether the UK is meeting that commitment.

chapters.title: Modern-slavery protections
chapters.takeaway: IOM argued that broad disqualification rules could deny victims individual assessment and support, while doing little to stop abuse of the system.

turns.speaker: Lord Rook
turns.text: The Bill would exclude some people from protection because of public-order concerns, criminal offences or alleged bad faith. What could that mean for trafficking victims and the UK’s legal obligations?

turns.speaker: Christa Rottensteiner
turns.text: The modern-slavery provisions could harm victims. The key question is whether excluding them is necessary and proportionate, and whether it fits the UK’s international obligations.

turns.speaker: Dr Patrick Burland
turns.text: Existing law already allows serious offenders to be excluded. The Bill could go further by excluding people given suspended sentences, even though a court decided their offence didn’t warrant prison. That raises a question about treating someone as safe to remain in the community but also as a serious threat.

turns.speaker: Dr Patrick Burland
turns.text: The Bill also appears to presume that people should be excluded on public-order grounds. A 2025 High Court ruling found that a presumption of this kind was incompatible with the treaty on human trafficking. Excluded people may also miss the full assessment needed to identify them as victims.

turns.speaker: Dr Patrick Burland
turns.text: Identifying victims helps protect them and supports investigations into traffickers. If traffickers see that people they exploit won’t get support, they may be able to operate more freely.

turns.speaker: Dr Patrick Burland
turns.text: There’s already a process for rejecting dishonest claims. Only 20 people were excluded for bad faith since 2023. But the Bill could treat someone as dishonest simply because they claimed to be a victim after being told they would be removed.

turns.speaker: Dr Patrick Burland
turns.text: Late claims aren’t all false: trauma can make victims disclose their experiences late, and the Government has accepted that some late claims are genuine. Only 36 people—about 0.15% of more than 23,000 referrals last year—would have been caught by the example of claims made after 11 pm before a planned removal.

turns.speaker: Dr Patrick Burland
turns.text: The rules could punish people for crimes committed as part of their exploitation. Two-thirds of victims excluded on public-order grounds had been referred as possible victims of criminal exploitation. For example, a woman forced into sex work might be excluded after being arrested for solicitation.

turns.speaker: Dr Patrick Burland
turns.text: That harms victims and could help traffickers. The committee should check whether the assumptions behind the Bill are supported by evidence. More training and more organisations able to refer victims quickly could improve the existing system without changing the law.

turns.speaker: Christa Rottensteiner
turns.text: Modern slavery and immigration can overlap, but they’re not the same issue. Many victims are British. Anti-slavery efforts work best when they focus on identifying and responding to exploitation.

chapters.title: Repaying asylum support
chapters.takeaway: UNHCR said charging recognised refugees for the support they needed while unable to work could be unfair and make it harder for them to become independent.

turns.speaker: Afzal Khan
turns.text: The Bill would let the Government require asylum seekers to repay the support they received. Is that compatible with the refugee convention?

turns.speaker: Vicky Tennant
turns.text: The Government has a legitimate interest in controlling costs. The better way to do that is to make decisions faster and fairly: the longer people remain in the system, the more it costs them and the state.

turns.speaker: Vicky Tennant
turns.text: We’re concerned that making recognised refugees repay support could breach the convention’s rule against imposing extra charges on refugees just because they are refugees. Asylum seekers often can’t work and have to rely on support to avoid destitution. UK nationals in similar need aren’t expected to repay equivalent help.

turns.speaker: Vicky Tennant
turns.text: The practical impact matters too. A refugee starting a new life, perhaps with a family, could face a debt of up to £10,000 per person. That would make it harder to find work, become self-sufficient and contribute.

chapters.title: Safe routes and what should change
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses welcomed new routes but said they must grow and sit alongside access to asylum, family reunion and improvements to the way decisions are made.

turns.speaker: Tom Gordon
turns.text: Are the new safe routes enough to provide an alternative to unauthorised entry, or to address concerns about the rest of the reforms?

turns.speaker: Vicky Tennant
turns.text: We welcome reopened resettlement and the new sponsorship plans, and UNHCR is helping to deliver them. But there should be several routes, not just one. Family reunion had helped many women and children from conflict zones and precarious situations; we’ve urged the Government to reopen it.

turns.speaker: Vicky Tennant
turns.text: Safe routes won’t meet everyone’s needs. People also need real alternatives in the countries they’ve fled to or are travelling through. For example, more Sudanese people are reaching the UK because they can’t find protection or opportunities where they are. And safe routes don’t replace the right to ask for asylum in the UK.

turns.speaker: Christa Rottensteiner
turns.text: IOM welcomes the new routes and is helping the Government design them. A range of options, including sponsorship, work and study, is important. We’ve seen the effect when family reunion falls: people we helped reunite with their families through the Red Cross have been affected, and fewer legal options can encourage dangerous journeys.

turns.speaker: Baroness Hamwee
turns.text: How many people might the sponsorship route help, and when will applications open?

turns.speaker: Vicky Tennant
turns.text: The Government has spoken of hundreds of places a year initially. Student applications are expected to open soon so people can arrive by next autumn; applications for the other routes are targeted for spring. We’re working with the Government and civil society to get the routes running and increase their scale.

turns.speaker: Lord Rook
turns.text: Apart from expanding community sponsorship, what should the committee recommend about the Bill and the wider policies?

turns.speaker: Christa Rottensteiner
turns.text: The committee should examine whether the claim that rising referrals show misuse is supported by evidence. We also think better training for organisations that identify victims, and faster referrals into the National Referral Mechanism (NRM), could improve the current system.

turns.speaker: Vicky Tennant
turns.text: We’ve raised concerns about refugee protection, long waits for settlement, family reunion and repayment of asylum support. For the new appeals body, it will be important to have expert decision-makers, consistent and high-quality decisions, and transparency, independence and oversight.
